subthemes.text:
Background

[3] The Appellant is a 58 year-old woman who fears her husband in Zimbabwe. She alleges that she endured decades of violence by her husband and lived in fear of him. She also alleges that her four adult children witnessed and experienced her husband's abuse. The Appellant fears further violence from her husband and his friends if she were to return to Zimbabwe.

[4] The Appellant applied for and received a visa to the United States (US) and travelled to the US with the intention of making a refugee claim in Canada. She made a claim for refugee protection in July 2018.
Determination

a. In its assessment of the Appellant's risk in Bulawayo, the proposed IFA;

I find the RPD erred in its analysis, and I find the Appellant to be credible in her testimony. I do not find that the Appellant has an IFA in Bulawayo, and she has rebutted the presumption of state protection.

subthemes.text:
[11] In my analysis of the appeal, I find that there are two significant considerations that the RPD failed to make in its IFA analysis. The first is the Appellant's desire to file for divorce from her husband. This is a fundamental right of hers and a core aspect of her right to self-determination. Should she pursue this and, if she were to return to Zimbabwe, I find that there is a serious possibility of being located and persecuted by her husband. For this reason, the IFA fails on the first prong of the IFA test.

[12] While this is in and of itself a sufficient reason to accept the appeal, I do not wish to ignore the Appellant's emotional and mental health in asking her to relocate to an IFA. This is in light of the psychological assessment that formed part of the RPD record2, and Ms. XXXX own testimony of the impact of enduring years of abuse. These facts lead me to find that any proposed IFA is unreasonable.

[13] In my analysis, I will first address the credibility issues raised by the RPD and then go on to analyze why the RPD erred in its IFA analysis.
The Appellant was credible

[14] Having independently reviewed the RPD record and hearing, I find the Appellant was credible with respect to all aspects of her claim, on a balance of probabilities.

[15] While the RPD also accepted the Appellant's credibility with respect to her allegations of domestic violence, the RPD found that the Appellant was lacking in credibility with respect to her testimony of her husband's political involvement, undermining her argument that she does not have an IFA.

[16] The RPD found that the Appellant, when questioned on her husband's work, omitted discussing her husband's political activities, a central aspect to her Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative. I see no omission. The Appellant reasonably explained that she distinguished between her husband's work and his political involvement. This is a reasonable and credible explanation in my view.

[17] The RPD also found the Appellant's testimony about her husband's political activities and ties to the ZANU-PF to be vague and inconsistent. Again, I cannot agree. She explained her limited knowledge of his political activities. Furthermore, her testimony needs to be considered in relation to her overall allegations; that she endured years of violence at the hands of her husband, and that she lived in fear. Her testimony must be considered through the lens of the Gender Guidelines 3. As a victim of gender-based violence the Gender Guidelines specifically addresses the depth of knowledge women may have in such circumstances:
Women from certain cultures where men do not share the details of their political, military or even social activities with their spouses, daughters or mothers may find themselves in a difficult situation when questioned about the experiences of their male relatives4

[18] Considering the social, emotional, cultural, and economic context the Appellant describes in her BOC, and in her testimony, I do not agree with the conclusion made by the RPD that the Appellant was inconsistent in her testimony. I accept the Appellant's description of her husband's work, political involvement, and connections.
The Appellant's desire to divorce is a fundamental right

[19] The RPD identified Bulawayo as a proposed IFA for the Appellant. I do not agree with the RPD analysis of the risk the Appellant faces in the proposed IFA. Rather, I find that based upon the Appellant's stated desire to divorce her husband, and the specific facts of this case, this places her at risk in any proposed IFA.

[20] During the hearing, Ms. XXXX stated that she did not want to remain married to her husband. Her counsel asked her what steps were required if she did not want to be married and the Appellant responded that she would need to file for divorce. Ms. XXXX then confirmed that her husband would have knowledge of her divorce filing, as he would be required to attend court for the proceedings.

[21] Counsel submitted that the requirement to serve your spouse when initiating a divorce proceeding is similar to court proceedings in Canada. The distinction is that in Canada, should the Appellant choose to file for divorce pursuant to the Divorce Act5 and alert her husband of her location, police protection is available, and she would be separated from him by the distance between the two countries (Canada and Zimbabwe). During her oral submissions, counsel emphasized that Ms. XXXX has the right to divorce and that the process of divorce in Zimbabwe would alert her husband to her location. While there is little objective evidence in the National Documentation Package (NDP) on the subject of divorce in Zimbabwe, there is evidence that even obtaining it comes with stigmatization and discrimination, "married women are regarded as more respectable than single or divorced women," and [that] divorce is often seen as "a failure on the part of the wife, resulting in her stigmatisation"6

subthemes.text:
[22] I have considered how the Appellant's desire for a divorce may also exacerbate the violence as it was her evidence that she received threats from her husband in the past when she raised the issue of separation.7 The question of the implications and risks related to Ms. XXXX seeking a divorce was not addressed in the RPD reasons.

[23] The right to choose one's marital status is a fundamental right pursuant to international and Canadian law. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights states as follows:
Article 16
(1) Men and women of full age, without any limitation due to race, nationality
or religion, have the right to marry and to found a family. They are entitled
to equal rights as to marriage, during marriage and at its dissolution.
(2) Marriage shall be entered into only with the free and full consent of the
intending spouses.
(3) The family is the natural and fundamental group unit of society and is
entitled to protection by society and the State.

[24] The Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women similarly states:
Article XVI
1. States Parties shall take all appropriate measures to eliminate discrimination against women in all matters relating to marriage and family relations and in particular shall ensure, on a basis of equality of men and women:
a. The same right to enter into marriage;
b. The same right freely to choose a spouse and to enter into marriage only with their free and full consent;
c. The same rights and responsibilities during marriage and at its dissolution...

[25] I find that Ms. XXXX expressed desire to divorce her husband is a core aspect of her right to self-determination. In Calderon v. Canada8 Justice Near found that the RPD's findings of IFA, in a case involving domestic violence and the custody of children, were "unduly harsh and unreasonable" where the RPD required that the Applicant not attempt to regain custody of her children. This is explained in para. 22 of the decision:

[22]The Respondent also argues that this is not a case of family members being separated, but a situation where the Applicant disagrees with a Mexican court order. However, the basis of the conditions of the IFA being unreasonable are the threats of the ex-husband to harm the Applicant if she attempts to assert her legal rights - the right to re-gain custody of her children. The Board held the Applicant and her claims of abuse and threats by her ex-husband to be credible. Therefore, while the separation was initiated by the custody order, it is perpetuated by the Applicant facing threats of violence from her ex-husband if she attempts to re-gain custody.[emphasis added]

[26] In the case before me I find Ms. XXXX in an analogous situation. That it would be unreasonable to expect her not to assert her right to a divorce in order to avoid being located and targeted in an IFA.

[8]On the issue of whether an IFA anywhere in Ghana is reasonable, I find that to properly apply the Chairperson's Gender 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution it was incumbent on the Member to consider the emotional impact on the Applicant of being required to live her life in the fear that, at any moment, she could be confronted by the violent predator. I believe that my previously expressed view on this issue is apt: for the Member to properly take the Guidelines into account in deciding the IFA issue in the present case, before placing any expectations on the Applicant, it was necessary for the Member to judge any potential expectation against the reality of the Applicant's life, including the tremendous upset she suffered as a result of the extreme violence she endured (see: Perez v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration),2006 FC 425, para. 8). Unfortunately, the Member's sensitive treatment of the Applicant's claim did not extend to this consideration.

[30] In this case, requiring the Appellant to relocate despite it being well documented and articulated that she would have to live in continual fear is unreasonable. For this reason, as well, the Appellant does not have an IFA.
The Appellant has rebutted the presumption of state protection

[31] Over the course of 38 years of marriage, the Appellant recounted numerous instances of reporting the violence to the police. When asked if the police ever did anything, she testified that "they didn't do anything to him." 11 She provided a copy of a police and medical report from an incident that took place in 2010.12 She also recounted instances where she told her family about the violence.

[32] The objective evidence indicates that Zimbabwe does have legislation that specifically addresses domestic violence. The legislation, enacted in 2007, stipulates that domestic violence is a crime and can result in imprisonment. Despite key gains by women's organizations to enact legislation and the resulting networks of shelters and services, the evidence indicates that it is largely still stigmatized in Zimbabwe:
"[t]here is reluctance by some police and judicial officers to implement and enforce legislation on domestic violence and rape" (Womankind 2011). Citing a 2012 Domestic violence, including legislation; state protection and support services available to... 9/17 ZWE105170.E 10 study by Musasa, an NGO that focuses on domestic violence, the Herald, lists several problems Zimbabwean women have experienced when reporting domestic violence to the police, including: police officers professing love to female victims of domestic abuse; authorities insisting that the victim bring the perpetrator with her to the police station; officers refusing service due to the belief that domestic violence should be handled privately; and police officers laughing while a victim makes her report (The Herald 13 Dec. 2012). Sources further report that there have been instances in which Zimbabwean police officers solicit bribes from victims of domestic violence in order to investigate or pursue cases (ibid.; Chuma and Chazovachii 2012, 11).13

REASONS FOR DECISION
Overview and decision
[1] These are my reasons for allowing the appeal of XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of Zimbabwe. I find that she is a Convention refugee.

[2] The Appellant had her claim heard by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) on October 31, 2019 and denied in a written decision on February 18, 2020. The Appellant appeals the decision of the RPD arguing that the RPD erred in its assessment of credibility and Internal Flight Alternative (IFA).
Background

[3] The Appellant is a 58 year-old woman who fears her husband in Zimbabwe. She alleges that she endured decades of violence by her husband and lived in fear of him. She also alleges that her four adult children witnessed and experienced her husband's abuse. The Appellant fears further violence from her husband and his friends if she were to return to Zimbabwe.

[4] The Appellant applied for and received a visa to the United States (US) and travelled to the US with the intention of making a refugee claim in Canada. She made a claim for refugee protection in July 2018.
Determination

[5] The appeal is allowed. The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its own determination that the Appellant is a Convention refugee.
Appellants arguments on appeal
[7] I have applied the correctness standard of review1.

[8] I have listened to the RPD hearing and reviewed the RPD record. I have conducted my own independent assessment of the evidence. I find the RPD erred in its analysis, and I find the Appellant to be credible in her testimony. I do not find that the Appellant has an IFA in Bulawayo, and she has rebutted the presumption of state protection.

[10] The test for IFA is two-fold; that there is no serious possibility of persecution in the proposed IFA and conditions in the proposed IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable to move there, considering the specific needs of the claimant (Appellant).

[11] In my analysis of the appeal, I find that there are two significant considerations that the RPD failed to make in its IFA analysis. The first is the Appellant's desire to file for divorce from her husband. This is a fundamental right of hers and a core aspect of her right to self-determination. Should she pursue this and, if she were to return to Zimbabwe, I find that there is a serious possibility of being located and persecuted by her husband. For this reason, the IFA fails on the first prong of the IFA test.

[12] While this is in and of itself a sufficient reason to accept the appeal, I do not wish to ignore the Appellant's emotional and mental health in asking her to relocate to an IFA. This is in light of the psychological assessment that formed part of the RPD record2, and Ms. XXXX own testimony of the impact of enduring years of abuse. These facts lead me to find that any proposed IFA is unreasonable.

[13] In my analysis, I will first address the credibility issues raised by the RPD and then go on to analyze why the RPD erred in its IFA analysis.
The Appellant was credible
[14] Having independently reviewed the RPD record and hearing, I find the Appellant was credible with respect to all aspects of her claim, on a balance of probabilities.

[15] While the RPD also accepted the Appellant's credibility with respect to her allegations of domestic violence, the RPD found that the Appellant was lacking in credibility with respect to her testimony of her husband's political involvement, undermining her argument that she does not have an IFA.

[16] The RPD found that the Appellant, when questioned on her husband's work, omitted discussing her husband's political activities, a central aspect to her Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative. I see no omission. The Appellant reasonably explained that she distinguished between her husband's work and his political involvement. This is a reasonable and credible explanation in my view.

[17] The RPD also found the Appellant's testimony about her husband's political activities and ties to the ZANU-PF to be vague and inconsistent. Again, I cannot agree. She explained her limited knowledge of his political activities. Furthermore, her testimony needs to be considered in relation to her overall allegations; that she endured years of violence at the hands of her husband, and that she lived in fear. Her testimony must be considered through the lens of the Gender Guidelines 3. As a victim of gender-based violence the Gender Guidelines specifically addresses the depth of knowledge women may have in such circumstances:
Women from certain cultures where men do not share the details of their political, military or even social activities with their spouses, daughters or mothers may find themselves in a difficult situation when questioned about the experiences of their male relatives4

[18] Considering the social, emotional, cultural, and economic context the Appellant describes in her BOC, and in her testimony, I do not agree with the conclusion made by the RPD that the Appellant was inconsistent in her testimony. I accept the Appellant's description of her husband's work, political involvement, and connections.
The Appellant's desire to divorce is a fundamental right

[19] The RPD identified Bulawayo as a proposed IFA for the Appellant. I do not agree with the RPD analysis of the risk the Appellant faces in the proposed IFA. Rather, I find that based upon the Appellant's stated desire to divorce her husband, and the specific facts of this case, this places her at risk in any proposed IFA.

[20] During the hearing, Ms. XXXX stated that she did not want to remain married to her husband. Her counsel asked her what steps were required if she did not want to be married and the Appellant responded that she would need to file for divorce. Ms. XXXX then confirmed that her husband would have knowledge of her divorce filing, as he would be required to attend court for the proceedings.

[21] Counsel submitted that the requirement to serve your spouse when initiating a divorce proceeding is similar to court proceedings in Canada. The distinction is that in Canada, should the Appellant choose to file for divorce pursuant to the Divorce Act5 and alert her husband of her location, police protection is available, and she would be separated from him by the distance between the two countries (Canada and Zimbabwe). During her oral submissions, counsel emphasized that Ms. XXXX has the right to divorce and that the process of divorce in Zimbabwe would alert her husband to her location. While there is little objective evidence in the National Documentation Package (NDP) on the subject of divorce in Zimbabwe, there is evidence that even obtaining it comes with stigmatization and discrimination, "married women are regarded as more respectable than single or divorced women," and [that] divorce is often seen as "a failure on the part of the wife, resulting in her stigmatisation"6

[22] I have considered how the Appellant's desire for a divorce may also exacerbate the violence as it was her evidence that she received threats from her husband in the past when she raised the issue of separation.7 The question of the implications and risks related to Ms. XXXX seeking a divorce was not addressed in the RPD reasons.

[23] The right to choose one's marital status is a fundamental right pursuant to international and Canadian law. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights states as follows:
Article 16
(1) Men and women of full age, without any limitation due to race, nationality
or religion, have the right to marry and to found a family. They are entitled
to equal rights as to marriage, during marriage and at its dissolution.
(2) Marriage shall be entered into only with the free and full consent of the
intending spouses.
(3) The family is the natural and fundamental group unit of society and is
entitled to protection by society and the State.

[25] I find that Ms. XXXX expressed desire to divorce her husband is a core aspect of her right to self-determination. In Calderon v. Canada8 Justice Near found that the RPD's findings of IFA, in a case involving domestic violence and the custody of children, were "unduly harsh and unreasonable" where the RPD required that the Applicant not attempt to regain custody of her children. This is explained in para. 22 of the decision:

[22]The Respondent also argues that this is not a case of family members being separated, but a situation where the Applicant disagrees with a Mexican court order. However, the basis of the conditions of the IFA being unreasonable are the threats of the ex-husband to harm the Applicant if she attempts to assert her legal rights - the right to re-gain custody of her children. The Board held the Applicant and her claims of abuse and threats by her ex-husband to be credible. Therefore, while the separation was initiated by the custody order, it is perpetuated by the Applicant facing threats of violence from her ex-husband if she attempts to re-gain custody.[emphasis added]

[26] In the case before me I find Ms. XXXX in an analogous situation. That it would be unreasonable to expect her not to assert her right to a divorce in order to avoid being located and targeted in an IFA.

[27] I find that Ms. XXXX has a right to obtain a divorce, to choose her marital status, and live her life in dignity without legal connection to her abuser. I agree with the submissions made by counsel that had the RPD considered this issue, regardless of where the Appellant moves in Zimbabwe, the act of obtaining a divorce will alert the Appellant's husband of her whereabouts. For this reason, I find the Appellant would face a serious possibility of persecution in any proposed IFA.
Psychological impact affects the reasonableness IFA

[28] In reviewing the RPD reasons, the RPD panel failed to engage with the psychological assessment included in the Appellant's evidence. Had this been considered, it would have been clear its impact upon the reasonableness of the IFA. The assessment describes in detail the Appellant's "pervasive feelings of fear". The assessment describes the emotional and psychological impact that years of violence has wrought on her and her ongoing fear of violence that is directed towards her and her children.9 In my view, the experiences described by the Appellant are an important and decisive consideration in the context of determining whether the IFA is reasonable.
[29] In Nimako v. Canada,10 the Federal Court stated the following in respect of the reasonableness of IFA in the context of gender violence:

[8]On the issue of whether an IFA anywhere in Ghana is reasonable, I find that to properly apply the Chairperson's Gender 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution it was incumbent on the Member to consider the emotional impact on the Applicant of being required to live her life in the fear that, at any moment, she could be confronted by the violent predator. I believe that my previously expressed view on this issue is apt: for the Member to properly take the Guidelines into account in deciding the IFA issue in the present case, before placing any expectations on the Applicant, it was necessary for the Member to judge any potential expectation against the reality of the Applicant's life, including the tremendous upset she suffered as a result of the extreme violence she endured (see: Perez v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration),2006 FC 425, para. 8). Unfortunately, the Member's sensitive treatment of the Applicant's claim did not extend to this consideration.

[30] In this case, requiring the Appellant to relocate despite it being well documented and articulated that she would have to live in continual fear is unreasonable. For this reason, as well, the Appellant does not have an IFA.
The Appellant has rebutted the presumption of state protection

[31] Over the course of 38 years of marriage, the Appellant recounted numerous instances of reporting the violence to the police. When asked if the police ever did anything, she testified that "they didn't do anything to him." 11 She provided a copy of a police and medical report from an incident that took place in 2010.12 She also recounted instances where she told her family about the violence.

[32] The objective evidence indicates that Zimbabwe does have legislation that specifically addresses domestic violence. The legislation, enacted in 2007, stipulates that domestic violence is a crime and can result in imprisonment. Despite key gains by women's organizations to enact legislation and the resulting networks of shelters and services, the evidence indicates that it is largely still stigmatized in Zimbabwe:
"[t]here is reluctance by some police and judicial officers to implement and enforce legislation on domestic violence and rape" (Womankind 2011). Citing a 2012 Domestic violence, including legislation; state protection and support services available to... 9/17 ZWE105170.E 10 study by Musasa, an NGO that focuses on domestic violence, the Herald, lists several problems Zimbabwean women have experienced when reporting domestic violence to the police, including: police officers professing love to female victims of domestic abuse; authorities insisting that the victim bring the perpetrator with her to the police station; officers refusing service due to the belief that domestic violence should be handled privately; and police officers laughing while a victim makes her report (The Herald 13 Dec. 2012). Sources further report that there have been instances in which Zimbabwean police officers solicit bribes from victims of domestic violence in order to investigate or pursue cases (ibid.; Chuma and Chazovachii 2012, 11).13

[33] And according to the UK Home Office Report,
Domestic violence is illegal and punishable by a fine and a maximum prison sentence of 10 years. However, the authorities generally consider it to be a private matter and prosecutions have been rare. 35% of ever-married women aged 15-49 have experienced spousal violence (physical or sexual violence committed by their husband/partner). Abuse by a husband or partner is the most common form of gender-based violence. Domestic violence is reportedly relatively common throughout Zimbabwe, but varies in prevalence between areas. 14

[34] Quite apart from the objective evidence, the Appellant described in her BOC and associated evidence her attempts to seek and secure state protection over the course of many years. I find that the objective evidence further confirms the challenges described by the Appellant in her testimony and, therefore, find that the Appellant has rebutted the presumption of state protection.
Summary

[35] Having independently reviewed the evidence, I find the Appellant credible. Her evidence related to decades of abuse and her attempts and desire to get away from her abuser are credible. I do not find she has an IFA, and she has rebutted the presumption of state protection. For these reasons I allow her appeal and find her to be a Convention refugee.
Conclusion

[36] Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(b) and subsection 111(2) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA or Act)15, the appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Appellant is a Convention Refugee.
